grades.reason: Discusses file-level permissions and mmap drawbacks, not distinguishing absent page mappings from page-access permission failures.

grades.quote: When an instruction fetch or a misaligned memory access straddles a page boundary, two different address translations are involved. When a guest-page fault occurs in such a circumstance, the faulting virtual address written to `mtval` / `stval` is the same as would be required for a regular page fault.
grades.reason: Provides fault-address information useful for locating the problematic mapping, but does not distinguish missing mappings from permission failures.

grades.quote: PTE_V indicates whether the PTE is present: if it is not set, a reference to the page causes a page fault (i.e., is not allowed). PTE_R controls whether instructions are allowed to read to the page. PTE_W controls whether instructions are allowed to write to the page. PTE_X controls whether the CPU may interpret the content of the page as instructions and execute them. PTE_U controls whether instructions in user mode are allowed to access the page; if PTE_U is not set, the PTE can be used only in supervisor mode.
grades.reason: Directly identifies the presence bit and access-permission bits to examine when distinguishing the two causes.

grades.quote: When SUM=0, S-mode memory accesses to pages that are accessible by U-mode (U=1 in Figure 67) will fault. When SUM=1, these accesses are permitted. SUM has no effect when page-based virtual memory is not in effect, nor when executing in U-mode. Note that S-mode can never execute instructions from user pages, regardless of the state of SUM.
grades.reason: Explains access-control conditions that cause permission faults, but does not explain how to identify an absent mapping.
